title: China warns World Court of 'overreach' after Rohingya genocide ruling, defends its judge
dek: Beijing, Myanmar's main backer, said it had concerns about the court exceeding its jurisdiction. Asked whether its national on the bench took instructions, it said she acted independently. It also told Japan again to correct its Taiwan remarks.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
China said on Friday that it had "concerns regarding such issues as ultra vires jurisdiction and overreach in interpretation" after the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled that Myanmar had committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, a judgment that bears directly on Bangladesh and India. It was Beijing's first comment on Thursday's ruling, the first time the UN's highest court has found any state responsible for genocide.

"China has noted the judgment of the International Court of Justice," the foreign ministry spokesman, Guo Jiakun, said at his regular briefing in Beijing, according to the ministry's transcript. He said the Rakhine State issue, "given its complex historical, ethnic and religious dimensions", needed to be resolved "prudently through a holistic approach", and that the international community should "avoid complicating the issue". International courts, he said, "should exercise their powers with full prudence in accordance with law."

## The question about China's judge

A reporter put it to Mr Guo that the Chinese judge on the court, Xue Hanqin, had "voted in Myanmar's favor on all but one count", and asked whether she had acted on instructions from the Chinese government. He did not answer directly. ICJ judges "serve in their individual capacity and perform their duties independently", he said, and Judge Xue's views were "grounded in international law and the facts of the case, and informed by her expertise."

Reports differ on the exact votes. The court's central finding of genocide was carried by nine votes to six, according to reports, with Judge Xue among the dissenters. Judge Xue, a former Chinese foreign ministry legal adviser and ambassador, was also the only judge to dissent when the court ruled in 2022, by 15 votes to one, that The Gambia could bring the case at all. The court's website could not be reached to confirm the full voting record.

China says it will "play a constructive role" in the repatriation of Rohingya refugees from Bangladesh. It has tried before: a China-brokered pilot plan to return a few thousand refugees to Rakhine in 2023 did not go ahead, after the refugees said conditions for a safe return did not exist, according to reports at the time. Beijing has kept close ties with Myanmar's military government since the 2021 coup, as has Russia, and both hold vetoes on the UN Security Council, the body The Gambia could ask to enforce the judgment if Myanmar does not comply.

## Why it matters for India and Bengal

China has large economic interests in Rakhine, where the Rohingya lived. It is developing a deep-sea port at Kyaukphyu on the Rakhine coast, the starting point of oil and gas pipelines that run to China's Yunnan province and give Beijing a route for energy imports that avoids the Strait of Malacca. India's own Kaladan transit project, which links Kolkata by sea to Sittwe port in Rakhine and on to Mizoram, runs through the same contested state.

Bangladesh shelters more than a million Rohingya in camps around Cox's Bazar. Any international push for their safe return will depend heavily on Beijing, Myanmar's largest neighbour and, with Russia, one of its main arms suppliers. If China uses its influence to shield the military from the ruling's consequences, the refugee burden on Bangladesh, and the pressure on the India-Bangladesh border along West Bengal, is unlikely to ease. India's Ministry of External Affairs has not commented on the judgment.

## Taiwan and Japan

At the same briefing, Mr Guo kept up pressure on Tokyo over Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's November 2025 remark that a Chinese blockade of Taiwan could threaten Japan's survival. Ms Takaichi had told reporters at the APEC summit in Shenzhen that Japan's position on Taiwan remained consistent with the 1972 Japan-China Joint Statement, according to reports. Mr Guo said that sticking to the four political documents between the two countries was Japan's "political responsibility and legal obligation", which should be shown "through concrete actions", and that Japan's urgent task was to correct its "erroneous words and moves on the Taiwan question". Japan has refused to withdraw the remark.

Mr Guo also said China opposed any international court that violated "the principle of state consent", abused its jurisdiction or applied "double standards", when asked about language on the International Criminal Court in this week's declaration by the leaders of China, Russia and the United States.
